title: API contract: ChatBackend foundation methods (create/update/destroy_object) have skeletal docs missing 5 critical implementer contracts
description:
## Finding

The three foundation methods on `ChatBackend` — `create_object`,
`update_object`, `destroy_object` (backend.rs:296-328) — have
docs of 2/3/1 sentences respectively, contrasting sharply with the
60-line specialized methods later in the same trait
(`apply_space_patch` at 503-571, `expire_message` at 830-892,
`generate_invite_code` at 336-414, etc., all exemplary).

```
/// Create a new object.
///
/// Returns `(assigned_id, created_object)` on success. `create_id` is the
/// client-side creation id used in the `/set` request.
fn create_object<O: SetObject + Send + Sync>(...) -> ...;

/// Apply a partial update (patch) to an existing object.
///
/// Returns `Some(updated_object)` if the backend modified any properties
/// beyond what the client requested (RFC 8620 §5.3 server-set field echo),
/// or `None` if the patch was applied verbatim.
fn update_object<O: SetObject + Send + Sync>(...) -> ...;

/// Destroy an existing object by id.
fn destroy_object<O: SetObject + Send + Sync>(...) -> ...;
```

## What goes wrong for a third-party implementer

A 50-line custom backend implemented from these docs alone would
silently mis-implement at least five contracts. None compile-fail,
none are caught by the kit's own MemoryBackend smoke tests, but
all manifest as spec-incorrect wire behaviour at runtime:

1. **SetErrorType selection for unknown account / unknown id /
   create_id collision is unstated.** `BackendSetError::Other(E)`
   vs `BackendSetError::SetError(SetError::with_type(AccountNotFound))`
   vs NotFound — the implementer has to read RFC 8620 §5.3 directly
   to choose. Wrong choice → wrong wire-level error → client cannot
   distinguish failure modes.

2. **Verbatim vs echo semantics for `update_object` return.** The
   doc says \"Some if backend modified beyond what client requested.\"
   But any backend that bumps `updatedAt` / `lastSeenAt` /
   membership counters on every successful update never hits the
   `None` branch. So either the `None` branch is dead, or
   \"beyond what client requested\" excludes server-bookkeeping
   timestamps — the implementer guesses inconsistently.

3. **State-bump contract for /changes is implicit.** Every successful
   create/update/destroy MUST bump the type's state token so
   `Type/changes` sees the mutation. The doc is silent. A backend
   that forgets ships `/changes` calls that miss writes.

4. **Cascade rules for `destroy_object` are unstated.** Destroying
   a `Space` — does the backend cascade to child `Messages`,
   `Roles`, `ReadPositions`? Destroying a `Role` referenced by
   `Member.role_ids` — `Err(SetError(InUse))` or successful with
   a hidden side effect? Contrast with `expire_message` at line
   885 which spends 60 lines explicitly documenting cascade.

5. **Atomicity within a single `update_object` call with
   multi-field patch is unstated.** All-or-nothing? Or
   field-by-field? The implementer cannot tell.

## Why this matters more than other doc gaps

`create_object` / `update_object` / `destroy_object` are the
most-used methods in `ChatBackend` — every `/set` call routes
through one of them. Spec-incorrect implementations here drop
straight to wire output. The asymmetry between these and
`apply_space_patch`'s 60-line doc is by itself a contract
defect: implementers expect doc weight to track method
importance, and here it's inverted.

## Recommendation

Add a 40-60 line doc block to each of the three methods covering
the five contracts above. Cross-reference RFC 8620 §5.3 explicitly
for SetErrorType selection. The single highest-leverage doc
change suggested by the 3rd-pass consumer-perspective exercise.

## Engineering basis

Verified by reading the rustdoc text on each of the three methods
(backend.rs:296-328) and noting what a third-party implementer
would have to either guess or read elsewhere. This is the
\"50-line custom backend exercise\" the 1st-pass and 2nd-pass
api-contract confidence notes both called out as the highest-
leverage missing exercise.
